Look, for example, at the book of Khalifah ibn Khayyat Shabab entitled Kitāb al-Tārīkh, and his other book entitled al-Ṭabaqāt; and likewise the Kitāb al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā of Muhammad ibn Saʿd, the scribe of al-Waqidi; and likewise the Sīrah of Ibn Ishaq; and likewise Nasab Quraysh of Musʿab ibn Abd Allah ibn Thabit al-Zubayri; and the book Jamharat Ansāb Quraysh of al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar; and what was composed after that of books on the Prophetic biographies.

And note that the people of hadith likewise had the precedence in this field, for they are the ones who placed dedicated chapters in their books. Al-Bukhari and Muslim and others placed in their books a Book of Virtues (manāqib) and a Book of Merits (faḍāʾil), and likewise the hadiths of the prophets. In the Merits they mentioned the merits of the Prophet (ṣ) and what God honoured him with, and in the Virtues the virtues of his Companions and his household and what has come in praise of them and concerning their high station.

Among the best of the books introducing the Prophet (ṣ) is the book al-Shifā bi-Taʿrīf Ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā of the Qadi Abu al-Fadl Iyad ibn Musa ibn Iyad al-Yahsubi al-Andalusi al-Sabti, may God have mercy on him. Of this book the people of knowledge said, when they read it: "Were it not for al-Shifā, al-Muṣṭafā (ṣ) would not have been known." It is a book which no student of knowledge can do without reading and reviewing.

We found our shaykhs, may God have mercy on them, reading it in this month, which is the month of Rabiʿ al-Awwal — which is in fact a Prophetic month, because the Prophet (ṣ) was born in it, and revelation began in it, because the truthful dream began in this month, and he emigrated in it, and died in it; so it is in fact a Prophetic month. For that reason we found our shaykhs reading the book al-Shifā in this month. I heard it thirteen times from Shaykh Muhammad Ali, may God have mercy on him, in this month. Many of the people of knowledge make it obligatory upon their students to read it, so that they may become acquainted with the Prophet (ṣ) and so that their conduct and their manners towards the Prophet (ṣ) may be refined and they may know his right and his station.

Among the affecting chapters in this book is the saying of the Qadi, may God have mercy on him: "Chapter on the greatness of his station (ṣ) and what is obligatory of revering and honouring him." From Malik, may God have mercy on him, he said: "If you had seen what I have seen, you would have laughed little and wept much. I lived to see Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, and he was a man of playfulness, but when the Messenger of God (ṣ) was mentioned in his presence he wept until it was as though he did not know you and you did not know him. And I lived to see Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, and when he related to us from the Messenger of God (ṣ) he wept until we had pity on him and left him."

And Malik would not wear sandals nor leather socks in Medina, out of reverence for the Messenger of God (ṣ). One day he went out to al-ʿAqiq and a man asked him about a hadith, and he said: "Who is this who asks about a hadith of the Messenger of God (ṣ) in the road?" and he ordered him to be flogged twenty lashes. It was said to him: "O Abu Abd Allah, he is the judge." He said: "The judge is the one most worthy of being disciplined", and he flogged him twenty lashes. Then when Malik went to his house he called him and had mercy on him and related to him twenty hadiths — a hadith in place of each lash. And the judge said: "Would that he had flogged me a hundred, so that he might have related to me a hundred hadiths."

They loved the Prophet (ṣ) with a deep and most affecting love. Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, went out one night in Medina and heard an old woman of the Helpers repeating these verses: "Upon Muhammad be the blessing of the pious; // upon him the good and the excellent have prayed. // You were one much given to standing, much weeping in the last hours of night. // Would that I knew — and deaths are of many turns — // will the abode bring me and my beloved together?" And Umar sat weeping at her door until the caller to prayer gave the call.

Likewise Ali, may God be pleased with him, made the two leaves of his door only at al-Manāṣiʿ, out of respect for the Prophet (ṣ). When he built his house he wanted to make two leaves for it, and he made them only at al-Manāṣiʿ, which is a piece of ground a mile from the Sanctuary of Medina, out of respect for the Prophet (ṣ), so that no voice should be raised over him in Medina.

God, glorified and exalted, confirmed this respect in His Book, and made its opposite something that nullifies deeds — we ask God for safety and well-being. He, exalted be He, said: {O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger, and fear God; truly God is Hearing, Knowing. O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not be loud in speech to him as you are loud to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you do not perceive. Truly those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of God — those are the ones whose hearts God has tested for God-consciousness; for them is forgiveness and a great reward. Truly those who call out to you from behind the chambers — most of them do not use their reason; and had they been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them; and God is Forgiving, Merciful} (Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt 49:1-5).

His Companions (ṣ) reached, in revering and honouring him, what Urwah ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi reported of them when he came to him at al-Hudaybiyah. He sat before him addressing him and found him performing ablution, and he would stretch out his hand towards the face of the Prophet (ṣ), saying: "O Muhammad, your people have brought along the milch camels with their young and have put on the skins of leopards, making a covenant with God that you shall never enter it upon them by force" — while the Messenger of God (ṣ) smiled. And he said: "I see with you nothing but a mixed rabble of people who are likely to flee from you and leave you."

Abu Bakr was with him and said to him: "Suck the clitoris of al-Lāt! Woe to you — would we flee and leave the Messenger of God (ṣ)?" He said: "Who is this?" It was said to him: "Abu Bakr." He said: "By God, were it not for a favour of yours towards me which I would have repaid you with — but this is for that."

And a man was standing over the head of the Prophet (ṣ), and whenever he stretched his hand towards his face he struck the back of his hand with the sword and said: "Keep your hand away from the face of the Prophet (ṣ)." He said: "O Muhammad, who is this standing over your head with the weapon?" He said: "This is your brother's son, al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah." And on that day nothing of the men could be seen but the pupils of the eyes beneath the mail-rings.

So Urwah returned astonished at what he had seen. He came to Quraysh and they received him, and he said: "O assembly of Quraysh, by God I have visited Chosroes in his kingdom and Caesar in his kingdom and the Negus in his kingdom, and I have not seen a king whose companions revere him as the companions of Muhammad revere him. By God, they are with him as though upon their heads were birds; and when he speaks they hasten to his command; and when he performs ablution they almost fight one another over his ablution water; and he does not spit but that it falls into the palm of one of them and he rubs his face and his head with it. And by God, they do not lift their eyes to him, out of awe of him."

This same description was reported to us by Amr ibn al-ʿAs as well, in what his son Abd Allah reported from him at his death. He said to him: "My son, three phases have passed over me. As for the first phase, when God sent His Messenger (ṣ) at Mecca there was no one on the face of the earth more intensely hated by me than he, and had I been able to harm him in anything I would have harmed him with it; and had I died in that phase I would have gone to the Fire. The second phase: after God cast faith into my heart, there remained no one on the face of the earth more beloved to me than the Messenger of God (ṣ), nor more majestic in my heart than he. And by God, I never filled my eyes with his face, out of shyness before him; and were I asked to describe him I could not describe him. And had I died in that phase I would have been in the Garden. Then after that came matters from which I wish I might come out even — neither against me nor for me."

So Amr was not able to describe the Prophet (ṣ), out of awe and reverence for him. Likewise Adi ibn Hatim, whom the Prophet (ṣ) used to bring near in his sitting and smile in his face, would ask afterwards whoever could describe him for him, and he said: "My eyes never had their fill of the face of the Prophet (ṣ)." And likewise Jarir ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali, whom the Prophet (ṣ) loved and brought near, used to say: "Truly the hours in which I saw the Prophet (ṣ) are more beloved to me than my lifetime, and I would wish that they were more. And the first thing I saw of him was the seal of prophethood; and were I asked to describe his face I could not describe it." And likewise al-Hasan ibn Ali, the grandson of the Messenger of God (ṣ) and the nearest of people to him, used to say to his maternal uncle Hind ibn Hind: "Describe the Messenger of God (ṣ) to me." And likewise a number of the Companions used to ask their brethren to describe the Prophet (ṣ) to them — because, out of the intensity of their respect for him, they did not look at him, and out of the intensity of their reverence likewise.

For this reason, when Khubayb ibn Adi, may God be pleased with him, was taken by the Banu Lihyan and sold at Mecca in the expedition of al-Rajiʿ, Quraysh put him in prison awaiting the end of the sacred month; and when the sacred month ended they took him outside the Sanctuary to kill him. When they brought him out and prepared the stake for him, Abu Sufyan came to him while he was shuffling in his irons, and said to him: "O Khubayb, you are of the Banu Jahjaba" — which is the clan among the Helpers that he belonged to — "and there is no kinship between us and you. Tell me: would you wish that Muhammad were with us in our hands, and that we did to him what you see, while you were with your family in well-being?" He said: "No, by God. It would not gladden me that Muhammad should be pricked by a thorn in the place where he is, and that I should escape what is in your hands." And when they placed him on the stake he raised his hands to God, glorified and exalted, and made an eloquent supplication and asked God to convey his greeting of peace to His Messenger (ṣ); and God conveyed his greeting of peace from him to His Prophet (ṣ) in that state.

Likewise what happened to Fatimah bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan when her menfolk were killed on the day of Uhud: her husband and her two sons and her father and her two brothers and her uncle and her father's uncle were killed — all of them killed on the day of Uhud before the Prophet (ṣ). When the Prophet (ṣ) came to Medina people came to greet him, and among those who came was Fatimah. She wanted to look at the face of the Prophet (ṣ), and people were coming between her and that; so the Prophet (ṣ) saw her and said: "Let her be." And when she drew near to him she looked at him and said: "May my father and my mother be your ransom, O Messenger of God. Every calamity after seeing you is a small thing." All calamities are a small thing, worth nothing, after seeing him (ṣ).

And likewise the case of Amr al-Usayrim, who is Amr ibn Thabit ibn Waqsh ibn al-Sakan, when his wounds became severe on the day of Uhud. Mahmud ibn al-Rabiʿ came to him and asked him, saying: "What brought you here, Amr — resentment on behalf of your people, or desire for Islam?" He said: "Rather desire for Islam. Convey my greeting of peace to the Messenger of God (ṣ)." And his greeting was conveyed to him.

And likewise the case of many of the Companions at such a time, at death: what they see does not distract them from love of the Prophet (ṣ); and likewise at grievous calamities. Indeed they reached such a degree in love of him (ṣ) that many of them were granted the doing of what the Messenger of God (ṣ) loved without his commanding them to it. It is established as sound in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Aisha, may God be pleased with her; she said: "We were in a night of biting cold and chill, and the Prophet (ṣ) said: 'Would that a righteous man of my community would guard me tonight from the Jews.' And while he was saying that, he heard the sound of weapons at the door. He said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'Saʿd ibn Malik' — Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. He said: 'And what brought you?' He said: 'I came to guard you, O Messenger of God.'" God chose them for His Messenger (ṣ) and granted them success in serving him, and so they used to act in this way.

Likewise the case of those who followed them after them: they reached this level of love of the Prophet (ṣ) and of holding him in awe and magnifying him, and magnifying his Companions and magnifying his household after him. Malik related to us from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad and from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, and these two are of the Followers, of the imams of the people of Medina. And likewise those after them of the best of this community: their eagerness to hear the hadith of the Prophet (ṣ) required of them long journeys to distant lands, and many of them would cross vast distances on their two feet — like Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who left no city to which a hadith of the Prophet (ṣ) had been transmitted but that he entered it, and who remained travelling for thirty-seven years gathering hadith. And his companion Yahya ibn Maʿin, who accompanied him on that whole journey, used to wish upon God that he might die in Medina; and God decreed that Yahya should die in the Rawdah, and that he should be washed upon the planks upon which the Prophet (ṣ) was washed, and that he should be buried in al-Baqiʿ. When Yahya died, the keeper of the Prophetic chamber said: "I shall bring out for you the planks upon which the Prophet (ṣ) was washed, so that you may wash Yahya upon them, because of his attachment to the hadith of the Prophet (ṣ)." So he brought out the planks for them and Yahya ibn Maʿin, may God have mercy on him, was washed upon them.

And likewise what there was among those after them of intense attachment to anything ascribed to the Prophet (ṣ) or that was of his furnishings or the goods of his house — they inherited that from the Companions of the Prophet (ṣ). This is Umm Salamah: as is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari, she had a small silver bell-vessel containing hairs from the hair of the Prophet (ṣ), and in it were holes; and when a person fell ill he would send her a cup of water, and she would dip the vessel into it for him, and he would drink it and be cured. The jiljil is a small vessel of silver like the one made into a bell.

And likewise Khalid ibn al-Walid had hairs from the hair of the Prophet (ṣ), and he used to put them in the helmet upon his head when he fought the enemy. And Muʿawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan had the Prophet's nail-clippings (ṣ); he kept them, and when death came upon him he directed that they be placed inside his eyelids, in his eyes, and that was done for him.

And likewise Abu Hurayrah had a sack which the Messenger of God (ṣ) gave him, containing measures of barley, and he kept spending from it for the rest of the life of the Prophet (ṣ) and the caliphate of Abu Bakr and the caliphate of Umar and the caliphate of Uthman. Then when Uthman was killed on the Day of the House, the house of Abu Hurayrah was plundered and that sack was taken from it; and he said, may God be pleased with him: "People have one grief, but I this day have two griefs: // the loss of the sack and the loss of the shaykh Uthman." So he began with it before Uthman, may God be pleased with him: his grief over it was more intense than his grief over Uthman, because of the intensity of his love for the Prophet (ṣ).

And likewise the caliphs of the Banu al-Abbas preserved everything that reached them of what had been the property of the Prophet (ṣ) or of his well-known Companions. They preserved the swords of the Prophet (ṣ) and a turban ascribed to him, and the swords and the turban are to this day in the exhibition at Istanbul. They were with the Abbasids, and when their state came to an end the Ottomans took them, and they remained with their sultans; and to this day the swords remain as they are, and part of the turban remains preserved with them up to our time. And likewise some of the letters which the Prophet (ṣ) wrote, such as his letter to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa and other letters.

And of the intensity of their attachment to the Prophet (ṣ) was their care for his traces, so much so that al-Mahdi ibn al-Mansur set up the pillars which were brought from Khurasan in the Sanctuary of Mecca as a marker of the Prophet's route (ṣ) to al-Safa, and had an inscription written upon them; and the four pillars still stand to this day in their place. He had written upon them — upon one of them the writing is still legible — the following: "The Commander of the Faithful Muhammad al-Mahdi ordered the placing of these two columns in this place as a marker of the route of the Messenger of God (ṣ) to al-Safa, so that the pilgrims to the House and its visitors may follow it. May God prolong the life of al-Mahdi, Commander of the Faithful, in magnification and honouring — and Musa and Harun. And that was in the year one hundred and sixty-seven, of the work of the people of Kufa." And this is still legible to our time, upon the column adjoining the House among the four columns; and upon the other columns the writing has remained but is no longer fully legible, as it was, on account of the ravages of time.

Likewise they took this from the Companions of the Prophet (ṣ), whose love for him was so intense that they would try to follow his traces even in what was not legislative among his acts. Thus Ibn Umar, when he went on the road of the Hajj or the ʿUmrah, would deliberately walk in the track of the Prophet (ṣ), so that he would turn aside from walking between two trees and would pass between two other trees, or would go round a tree. It was said to him: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I saw the Prophet (ṣ) when his she-camel bolted with him, and he did it" — so he does it. And he would make his she-camel kneel in a place and urinate there and say: "I saw the Prophet (ṣ) do it."

And the matter reached such a degree of care for this that even in the days of Urwah ibn al-Zubayr — and he is of the Followers — he relates concerning one of the expeditions which the Prophet (ṣ) undertook at the beginning of Islam, that he halted by a tree there and food was cooked for him: "and I have seen the trace of the fireplace" — "I have seen the trace of the fireplace." This is a complete care for the traces of the Prophet (ṣ) and the tracking of them: Urwah went so far as to see the fireplace of the fire that was kindled for the Prophet (ṣ) so that food might be cooked for him upon it — out of the intensity of the heart's attachment to him and love of him.

Among that too is the care for his household. Muslim brought out in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them and may He please them, that he said: "I entered among a group upon Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and he was old and had lost his sight. He said: 'Who are the people?' and they were identified to him until it reached me, and he said: 'O son of my brother, come near me.' So I drew near to him, and he stretched out his hand and undid my upper button and my lower button and placed his hand between my breasts, then said: 'O son of my brother, ask me whatever occurs to you.' And I said: 'I ask you about the pilgrimage of the Messenger of God (ṣ)'" — and he related to him the Farewell Pilgrimage at its full length; and this hadith is among the longest hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim. In this hadith it is mentioned that Jabir undid his upper button and his lower button and placed his hand between his breasts and drew him near and brought him close, because of his position in relation to the Prophet (ṣ) — for he is Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them all.

And likewise was their care for his household and for everyone between whom and him there was a connection. The Prophet (ṣ) in his lifetime used to visit Barakah, Umm Ayman, his freedwoman; and when Abu Bakr took charge of the caliphate he said to Umar: "Come, let us visit Umm Ayman as the Prophet (ṣ) used to visit her." So they went to her, and when they sat down Umm Ayman wept a great weeping. They said to her: "What makes you weep? Do you not know that what is with God is better for the Messenger of God (ṣ) than this world?" She said: "Indeed, I do not weep because I do not know that what is with God is better for His Messenger (ṣ) than this world; but I weep for the cutting off of the revelation." And she made them weep, and they wept a great weeping until they went out.

This love ought to continue among the believers, and to return now to what it was in the days of the Companions and the Followers, and to be purified of the impurities and the defilements that contravene the guidance and the sunnah.

For many people suppose that love of the Prophet (ṣ) consists in going to excess concerning him and describing him with what is not sound, of invented descriptions which the Prophet (ṣ) forbade, saying: "Do not extol me as the Christians extolled Jesus the son of Mary." Some people claim that part of love of him is to extol him and to describe him as being the secret of the existence of the whole world, and that but for him no sun and no moon would have been created, and other things of which the Prophet (ṣ) never gave any report, and which he taught to none of his Companions, and with which they never described him.

And likewise the taking of his grave as a festival: the Messenger of God (ṣ) forbade that and cursed whoever does it, and he directed that his grave not be taken as a festival and asked God that his grave not be taken as a festival. And the like of that is the taking of his birth as a festival, in imitation of the Christians who made the birth of Jesus a festival; and this too contravenes his sunnah and is not of his guidance nor of love of him. And the like of that is the invention of forged hadiths concerning seeking a means of access (tawassul) through him, or, more severe than that, concerning calling upon him for aid (istighāthah) (ṣ). For he came only to change association (shirk) and to wipe it out and efface it from the earth. And we bear witness that he conveyed the message and discharged the trust and counselled the community, and that there is no good but that he directed to it, and no evil but that he warned against it. So what the Prophet (ṣ) brought suffices us, and we have no need of any addition.

May God have mercy on Shaykh Bab ibn al-Shaykh Sidiyya, when he says: "Be a helper to the God, // and denounce the reprehensible things; // and be with the truth which // He is pleased with from you, turning wherever it turns; // and do not count as benefiting // or harming anything other than Him. // And travel the road of al-Muṣṭafā, // and die travelling upon it. // For what sufficed our first, // does it not suffice the last? // And be an emigrant from a people who have innovated // in his affair. // They have alleged allegations // and blackened registers, // and they have subdued the people of the wastes // and subdued the townsfolk; // and the elders have bequeathed // their innovation to the young ones. // And if a disputant calls // concerning their affair to a wrangling, // then do not wrangle over them // except an outward wrangling."

And he says also, may God have mercy on him: "Believe, my brother, and be upright, // and hold fast to the way of Ahmad; // and shun the paths — do not // let the tangled dreams delude you. // There is no good in a religion which, with // the best of generations, was non-existent, // which was innovated by one who did not come // with any certainty that he was preserved from error — // after 'Today I have perfected for you' // had been sent down, // and after there was established with // a gathering at Ghadir Khumm. // Call to his road — // be particular among people and be general; // and say, when they turn away: // 'Upon you is the care of your own souls.'"

Love of the Prophet (ṣ) is not by wishing, nor by false sayings, nor likewise by claiming and inventing what God has not given leave for. Indeed the Prophet (ṣ) said: "Lying against me is not like lying against anyone else; so whoever lies against me, let him enter the Fire."

And likewise I shall relate to you what my grandfather Muhammad Ali ibn Abd al-Wadud related to me. He said: Yahzih ibn Abd al-Wadud related to us, from Muhammad ibn Muhammad Salim, from Hamid ibn Umar, from al-Faqih al-Khattat, from the Qadi Ibn Aʿl Mamm al-Sibaʿi, from Shaykh al-Shuyukh al-Hasani, from Ali al-Ujhuri, from al-Burhan al-ʿAlqami, from al-Jalal al-Suyuti, from Zakariyya al-Ansari, from al-Hafiz Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani, from Ibrahim al-Balkhi, from Ahmad ibn Abi Talib al-Hajjar, from Abd al-Awwal ibn Isa al-Sijzi, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mubarak, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Dawudi, from Abd Allah ibn Ahmad al-Sarakhsi, from Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Matar al-Firabri, from Muhammad ibn Ismaʿil ibn Ibrahim al-Bukhari in his Ṣaḥīḥ. He said: al-Makki ibn Ibrahim related to us; he said: Yazid ibn Abi Ubayd informed us, from Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, that the Prophet (ṣ) said: "Whoever says of me what I did not say, let him take his seat in the Fire."

This hadith is the first of the three-link chains of al-Bukhari in the Ṣaḥīḥ: between al-Bukhari and the Prophet (ṣ) in it there are three persons — al-Makki ibn Ibrahim, and Yazid ibn Abi Ubayd the client of Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, and Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ who is the Companion.

So those who invent against the Prophet (ṣ) hadiths he did not say — these do not love him and do not realise this sought-after love. And those who call upon him apart from God have contravened what he brought entirely; for he came only to smash association and to demolish everything that is called upon apart from God, and he expended his effort in that and realised it, until God alone was worshipped upon this earth. So how can you make love of him consist in the contrary of what he brought and the contrary of his call entirely?

Likewise, love of the Prophet (ṣ) requires the learning of his sunnah. How, my brother, do you realise love of the Prophet (ṣ) while you have not read the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari nor the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim nor the Muwaṭṭaʾ of Malik, and have not looked into anything of the hadiths of the Prophet (ṣ), and have dispensed with that by what people have written? Can love of him be realised for you while you abandon his speech and do not read anything of his sunnah?

The Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, passed through many phases and stages; and when his term drew near he repented of all those phases and came out of them and returned to the sunnah of the Prophet (ṣ), and he died with the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari upon his breast, turning its pages.

Many people suppose, or allege, that they love the Messenger of God (ṣ) while they abandon his sunnah and do not wish to learn it at all, and content themselves in that with many of the formulas of prayer upon him which contain a great deal of exaggeration and rashness.

Among the most astonishing things I have heard in that regard is that a man of the senior officials in this state of ours — with our respect for the senior officials — met a man at Charles de Gaulle airport in Paris and asked him about his specialisation. He said: "Where do you study?" He said: "I study at such-and-such a university." He said: "In what specialisation do you study?" He said: "I study hadith." He said: "Astonishing — there is a specialisation called the specialisation of hadith?" He says to him: "I think that of hadith, the Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt that your mother has is enough; that much of hadith is sufficient."

This notion has spread among people until many people have come to suppose that hadith is merely those formulas of prayer containing much rashness which the Messenger of God (ṣ) never commanded, nor any of his Companions, nor any of the Followers, and which were not known in the first age of this community, and which the imams who exercised independent reasoning — those who are taken as models in the religion of God — did not know. Rather they are among the inventions of people afterwards; and these were made a substitute for the hadiths of the Prophet (ṣ) and were nominated in their place.

I now come, after the discussion of love of the Prophet (ṣ), to his pure qualities (shamāʾil). The shamāʾil means the traits and the descriptions, and what is meant by them is what has been transmitted from the Prophet (ṣ) of the descriptions of his physical form and of his character. They are included under the name "hadith" with the hadith scholars, and are not included under the name "hadith" with the jurists and the legal theorists. For hadith with the legal theorists is what has been transmitted from the Prophet (ṣ) of a saying or an act or a tacit approval that is fit to serve as evidence for a legal ruling — and this is hadith with the jurists also. But with the hadith scholars, hadith is what has been transmitted from the Prophet (ṣ) of a saying or an act or a tacit approval or a description of his physical form or of his character, whether or not it is fit to serve as evidence for a legal ruling; everything narrated from the Prophet (ṣ) is included under the name "hadith".

This definition ought to be restricted by a restriction which the hadith scholars do not mention, namely that the describer should have seen the Prophet (ṣ) — so as to exclude thereby the panegyrists who praise him with many descriptions though they did not see him; for their description of him is not hadith, even though it is a description of the Prophet (ṣ), because they did not see him. Therefore this should be what was transmitted of him by one who saw him: the definition should be restricted by its issuing from one who saw him (ṣ).

Those who saw him described him with many descriptions. As for the descriptions of his character, they are in the Book of God, glorified and exalted, and in it is enough of them. For God, exalted be He, said: {Nūn. By the pen and what they write down, you are not, by the blessing of your Lord, possessed; and truly for you is a reward unfailing; and truly you are upon a mighty character} (Sūrat al-Qalam 68:1-4). And God, exalted be He, says: {By the forenoon and by the night when it is still, your Lord has not forsaken you nor detested you; and the hereafter is better for you than the former; and your Lord shall surely give you, and you will be satisfied} (Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā 93:1-5). And He, exalted be He, says: {Did We not expand your breast for you, and lift from you your burden which weighed down your back, and raise high your mention for you?} (Sūrat al-Sharḥ 94:1-4). And He, exalted be He, says: {Truly We have granted you a clear victory, that God may forgive you what went before of your fault and what came after, and complete His favour upon you, and guide you to a straight path, and that God may help you with a mighty help} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:1-3).

And He, exalted be He, says: {Muhammad is the Messenger of God; and those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and good pleasure. Their mark is upon their faces from the trace of prostration. That is their likeness in the Torah; and their likeness in the Gospel is as a crop that puts forth its shoot and strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands upon its stalk, delighting the sowers — that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. God has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:29).

And He, exalted be He, says: {And My mercy embraces all things; and I shall write it for those who are God-conscious and give the alms-due and who believe in Our signs — those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel: he enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, and makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him and honour him and help him and follow the light that was sent down with him — those are the successful} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:156-157).

And likewise it has come in the hadith of Ibn Abbas in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi and elsewhere, with a sound chain, that the description of the Prophet (ṣ) in the Torah is that he is not coarse nor given to coarseness, nor one who shouts in the markets. These attributes are negative, and they establish their opposites, which is his being characterised (ṣ) by uprightness and justice and gentleness and mercy. And God, glorified and exalted, mentioned in His Book his being characterised by these qualities, in His saying: {There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what distresses you, full of concern for you, to the believers kind and merciful} (Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:128).

So these are his qualities of character (ṣ) in the Book of God; and of them it is enough to cite God's saying, exalted be He: {and truly you are upon a mighty character} — for he encompasses these qualities and gathers them. That is why one of our scholars says — I think it is Shaykh Muhammadhu ibn Habib al-Rahman, may God have mercy on them — he says: "After the praise of our Creator, exalted be He, // upon Ṭāhā, is there any praise left for creatures? No. // For 'upon a mighty character', emphasised, // has left no word for any creature to say." This is the praise of God the Creator, and that leaves no word for any creature.

And likewise among these descriptions is the description of him by al-Abbas, may God be pleased with him. He said to him: "O Messenger of God, will you permit me to praise you?" He said: "Say." And he said: "Before it you were goodly in the shadows and in // the place of deposit, where the leaves are sewn together. // Then you descended to the lands — you were not // a human being, nor a morsel of flesh, nor a clot, // but a drop that rode the ship when // drowning had bridled Nasr and his people. // You entered the fire of the Friend, hidden // in his loins — you: how could it burn? // He is transferred from loins to womb; // when one age passes, a new layer appears — // until your restraining house comprised // from Khindif a height beneath which are the girdles. // So we are in that radiance and in // the light, and through the paths of right guidance we cut our way."

Al-Abbas has set out the course of the Prophet (ṣ) and his passing among the prostrators from the time of Adam when he was sent down from the Garden, to the time of the Flood and Noah's boarding of the ark, to Abraham's being cast into the fire and his deliverance from it, to what came after that of the passing until he reached Khindif — who is the wife of Ilyas ibn Nizar ibn Maʿadd ibn Adnan, and she is the mother of Mudrikah, the ancestor of the Prophet (ṣ) — and he praised him with this praise of which he is worthy.

And he had been praised before with these descriptions of form and character likewise by Abu Talib, in his poem rhyming in lām composed in the mountain pass, concerning which Ubaydah ibn al-Harith ibn al-Muttalib said on the day of Badr: "If Abu Talib were alive he would know that we are more entitled than he to his saying: 'And we shall surrender him only when we are struck down around him // and are made forgetful of our sons and our wives.'" He is referring here to the saying of Abu Talib: "And one white of face, by whose countenance the rain-clouds are sought, // the sustenance of orphans, a refuge for widows. // The destitute of the family of Hashim take shelter with him, // and they are with him in blessing and bounties. // You have lied — by the House of God — that we would let Muhammad be seized // while we have not yet fought in his defence and striven. // And we shall surrender him only when we are struck down around him // and are made forgetful of our sons and our wives."

Those who described him among his Companions (ṣ) went in various directions in these descriptions. As for the side of character, the greatest description of him is what Aisha, may God be pleased with her, described him with when she was asked about the character of the Messenger of God (ṣ), and she said: "His character was the Qur'an." This is the most eloquent description and the most comprehensive and the greatest: "his character was the Qur'an" — everything God commanded, he realised it in his character; and everything He forbade, he avoided it; and there gathered in him what God was pleased with for His servants. For this God made him a righteous model for all people. This is the most comprehensive description of the Prophet's character (ṣ). If you wish to find his description in what pertains to character, read the Book of God: every command God commanded in His Book, he realised it; and every prohibition He forbade, he kept away from it; and every character trait He directed to, he realised it. And God prepared him for that and chose him: his breast was split open twice and the black morsel was brought out of it and its place was washed with the water of Zamzam, and He prepared him to be a model for all human beings.

Likewise on the side of physical form, a number of them described him. Among the descriptions upon which they agreed in describing him (ṣ) is that he was of middling height inclining to tallness — that is, neither conspicuously tall nor so short that eyes would look down upon him; he was of middling height inclining to tallness. And likewise in colour: he was neither of a stark, chalky whiteness, nor of a redness that eyes look down upon, but he was white tinged — that is, tinged with redness; his whiteness was tinged with redness.

And they described him likewise as having a face like a segment of the moon: it resembles a segment of the moon in roundness. And they described him likewise as having an aquiline nose, and fine-arched eyebrows, and long eyelashes; and what was between his two eyebrows was joined; and he was broad of forehead, and round in it. And he was likewise (ṣ) even in the setting of the mouth, and there was a space between his teeth — that is, no two of his teeth were touching. And he was of gleaming front teeth: when he smiled it was as though a lightning flash shone from his mouth.

And likewise he was large of bone-joints — that is, of the joints — mighty in the ends of the bones, that is, his joints were strong and firmly knit. And he was even-bodied, that is, his chest and his belly were level, so that his belly was not higher than his chest nor his chest higher than his belly; and this is the meaning of his being bādin. And likewise he was (ṣ) strong of body: when he walked it was as though he were going down a slope. Men would hurry and exhaust themselves to catch up with him while he did not force himself — that is, he did not force himself in walking; when he walked he went quickly. And when he turned, he turned with his whole body, and that was for dignity and gravity. Whoever saw him suddenly stood in awe of him, and often a person would be seized with trembling when he saw him suddenly for the first time, because of his awe-inspiring presence (ṣ). That is why he said to the man who came to him and, when he saw his face, was seized with al-buraḥāʾ, that is, sweat and trembling — he said to him: "Be at ease with yourself; I am not a king — I am only the servant of God and His Messenger."

And likewise they described him with regard to the fingers: that the fingers of his hands were even; and he was smooth of cheek; and he was thick-fleshed in the feet, and smooth-soled — that is, his two feet were not broad. And he was (ṣ) even of shins, that is, there was in them no crookedness and no swelling in one place rather than another. And likewise he was fine in the masrubah, which is the hairs that grow from the chest to the navel, so that it is a continuous line. And he was thick of beard; and he (ṣ) would trim the two ends of his moustache, and its fringe would appear as the finest of fringes appears — "its fringe", that is, the end of his moustache, would appear as the finest of fringes appears.

And he was deep black and white of eye, that is, intense in their blackness, intense in their whiteness: their white was intensely white and their black intensely black. And he (ṣ) would not change colour in heat nor in cold; on journeys his colour would not change, so that his colour was as it is in heat and in cold and in all states.

And likewise he was sweet of scent: people would smell the scent of perfume from his sweat (ṣ) when he had not put on perfume. Indeed Umm Sulaym would take his sweat and put it into perfume, and the people of Medina would say: "We have never seen a perfume better than her perfume", and they would ask her about her perfume, and she would say: "I have put into it the best of perfumes" — meaning the sweat of the Prophet (ṣ).

And likewise there was (ṣ) upon his back the seal of prophethood, and it was upon his left shoulder-blade, and it was like a pigeon's egg; at the top of it were hairs that grew upon it, so that it was like the warts which are of a colour between dustiness and blackness, and hairs had grown upon it. And this is the seal of prophethood of which the prophets before had given report and which they had made clear was his sign. And those who studied the earlier scriptures, when they greeted him, would go round behind his back to see the seal of prophethood; and he would sometimes occupy himself with a matter until his cloak fell from his back and people would see the seal of prophethood.

Likewise on the side of character: he was described with intense modesty, so that he was more modest than a virgin in her curtained chamber. And likewise he was the most humble of people: the black slave-woman would come to him and take him by the hand until he had settled her need for her. And the rough desert Arab would come to him and pull him by the edge of his garment until it left a mark on the side of his neck, saying: "O Messenger of God, order me something from the wealth of God that is under your hand" — and he would smile and settle his need for him.

And one day he had come forward to the prayer when a man came to him and stood before the row shouting and said: "O Messenger of God, teach me of what God has taught you"; and he was gentle with him and went to him and taught him at length while the people were in their rows, and then he came to his place and led the people in prayer and did not repeat the call to stand.

And likewise he would be at the service of his household, mending his sandal and sewing his garment and sweeping his house with his own hand (ṣ). And of the intensity of his humility was that he would lie upon a reed mat and its mark would remain in his ribs; and after that his bed was of tanned leather — that is, of red hide stuffed with palm fibre — and when a guest came he would seat him upon it.

And likewise, of his character (ṣ) was forbearance: he would not become angry except for the anger of God, when the sanctities of God were violated; and when he became angry nothing could stand before his anger. And likewise, of his description (ṣ) was patience under people's harm, so that he was the most patient of people.

And of his character (ṣ) likewise was generosity. In the hadith of Jabir: the Messenger of God (ṣ) was the most generous of people; he was never asked for anything and said "No" — if he had it he gave, and otherwise he answered with what was easy of speech. And in the hadith of Ibn Abbas, he said: the Messenger of God (ṣ) was the most generous of people, and he was at his most generous in Ramadan when Gabriel would meet him and study the Qur'an with him; and the Messenger of God (ṣ) was more generous with good than the sent wind.

And likewise he was (ṣ), out of the intensity of his concern for people, one who visited the sick, even among non-Muslims. He went to visit a Jewish boy who was ill and found him at the point of death, and said to him: "Say: there is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." And the boy raised his head to his father, seeking his permission in that, and he said: "Say what Abu al-Qasim has commanded you." So he said it and died. And the Prophet (ṣ) said to his Companions: "Take charge of your companion" — and they took him and prepared him, and the Prophet (ṣ) prayed over him and buried him.

And likewise, of the intensity of his humility was that he would answer every invitation to which he was invited. A Jew invited him to a dry loaf and rancid fat and he answered his invitation — "a nāssah loaf", that is, dry and hardened, "and ihālah", that is, butter, "sanikhah", that is, whose colour had changed so that it had yellowed — and he responded to that. And of his humility (ṣ) was that he said: "If I were invited to a trotter or a foreleg I would respond" — so he responds to whatever he is invited to.

And likewise he was (ṣ) much given to smiling; but when he smiled only his eye-teeth would appear, and he did not give himself up to laughter, and his voice was not heard in laughter.

And likewise, of his description (ṣ) was his keeping of kinship ties and his chastity: he was the most chaste of people and the most given of them to keeping ties with his relatives — so much so that Umm Salamah reminded him of that when he did not accept the pledge of allegiance of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, and she said: "Let not your cousin and your aunt's son be the most wretched of people because of you." And he did not accept her intercession, so they went to Ali seeking his intercession. He said: "I shall not intercede for you two, but I shall direct you to what is better than that." They said: "And what is it?" He said: "It is not fitting that anyone should be better in answer than the Messenger of God (ṣ). Say to him what the brothers of Joseph said to Joseph: {By God, God has indeed preferred you over us, and we were indeed wrongdoers} (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:91)." So they said that to him, and he said what Joseph, peace be upon him, said: {No reproach upon you this day; God will forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful} (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:92).

And likewise of his character (ṣ) was his mercy to the small and the weak and the poor. The little boys would come to him and play with the seal of prophethood. And he was praying when al-Husayn and Umamah came and mounted upon his back while he was prostrating, and he prolonged the prostration for them so as not to disturb them or to embarrass them; and when he gave the salutation he said: "What an excellent camel your camel is." And al-Hasan came to him while he was praying and stood at his side, and he carried him in his standing: when he bowed or prostrated he put him down, and when he stood he carried him. And he carried Umamah bint Abi al-ʿAs likewise in the prayer.

And of his mercy to small children was that he would play with them and joke with them. One day he entered the house of Abu Talhah and saw Abu Umayr playing with a little bird of his, and he said: "What has the little sparrow done, O Abu Umayr?" — and he gave him this kunyah while he was a small child, addressing him by the names most beloved to him.

And he used to do that even with his enemies. It is established as sound that when Utbah ibn Rabiʿah came to him disputing with him on behalf of Quraysh, he said to him: "Listen, Abu al-Walid", and recited to him Sūrat Fussilat until he reached God's saying, exalted be He: {But if they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamud} (Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:13); and he said: "Enough, enough" — and he silenced him.

And likewise he would show them good hospitality: he would show good hospitality to the Jews, and he showed good hospitality to ʿĀmir ibn al-Fitl and Arbad when they came to stay with him, despite their association of partners with God and their enmity to God and His Messenger.

And likewise, of his character with people was gentleness and mercy; and he was known for that among people, so much so that the Jews of the Banu Qurayzah, when he said to them "O brothers of apes and swine", said: "O Abu al-Qasim, we have not known you to be one who reviles."

And of his modesty (ṣ) before his Lord, mighty and majestic, was that it is reported that on the Day of the Conquest, when he entered Mecca with the weapons, he pressed his chin to his chest out of modesty before God, mighty and majestic.

And he wept much out of fear of God, mighty and majestic: he would weep in the standing of the night, and he stood a whole night reciting a single verse, which is God's saying, exalted be He: {If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, then truly You are the Mighty, the Wise} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:118). And he was likewise much given to supplication and to insistent appeal to God, glorified and exalted; and his stands in that are witnessed, as on the day of Badr and others, adjuring God by what He had promised.

These are some of the qualities of the Prophet (ṣ), and we cannot exhaust them all. Many books have been composed on them and have not contained a sufficient measure of them. And time is an enemy to us when it takes us out of the qualities of the Prophet (ṣ) — just as the learned Abd Allah ibn Sayyid Mahmud, may God's mercy be upon him, said when he went out of Medina on his pilgrimage and saw it behind his back: he turned towards it weeping and said: "The Messenger has departed, and his Tayyibah has gone far from you; // truly loved ones and homelands are enemies." Truly loved ones and homelands are enemies when they are a cause of a person's going out of the city of the Prophet (ṣ). And likewise time is an enemy to us when it takes us out of the qualities of the Prophet (ṣ).

And perhaps I shall conclude here with some verses from the poem of the learned Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad Salim al-Majlisi, may God have mercy on them all, where he says: "Does his eye scatter the scattered pearls // out of passion, from his remembering the dwelling places? // Dwelling places at al-ʿAqiq to al-Munqā, // to Uhud — the remembrance of them has grieved me. // And from the recollection of a lodging at Salʿ // to al-Jammā, it suffers what it suffers. // Is there then a resolve that will assault procrastination? // And is there, after the far separation, any drawing near? // And shall I set out at the birds' morning, my saddle // upon a strong-cheeked, firm-built, noble she-camel, // that outstrips the riding camels, her hind hooves treading in the tracks of the fore, // and folds up the wastes, tall-humped and lean? // You would see her, after persistence, like a wild ass // at Yamʾūd, braying over a she-ass, // urged on by longing for the abode of the Conquest, the refuge // of the leader of the messengers, the safe haven of every offender. // By your life, describe his qualities to me, for I // yearn for his beautiful qualities. // For neither the sun of noon on a cloudy day // resembles his two cheeks, nor comes near it; // nor does the full moon when it appears // resemble the face on the night of its fullness."

flags.arabic: وكذلك اتخاذ قبره عيدا فقد حرم ذلك رسول الله (ص) ولعن من فعله … ومثل ذلك اتخاذ مولده عيدا تأسيا بالنصارى … ومثل ذلك اختلاق الأحاديث الموضوعة في التوسل به، أو أشد من ذلك بالاستغاثه به (ص)
flags.context: The section on the controls of love: the practices the Sheikh rejects as excess (ghuluww).
options: Translate the position in full and exactly, flagging it as editorially sensitive
Soften the terms ('some scholars hold…')
Omit the passage
flags.note: EDITORIAL, and the single most consequential passage in the record. The Sheikh states plainly that taking the Prophet's grave as a festival is forbidden and cursed; that taking his birth (mawlid) as a festival imitates the Christians and contravenes the sunnah; and that hadiths invented about tawassul through him, and a fortiori istighāthah (calling upon him for aid), are fabrications. He also rejects the 'secret of existence' / 'but for you' (lawlāka) formulations. These are live and contested positions, and the lecture itself was delivered in Rabīʿ al-Awwal — which he describes as a Prophetic month for other reasons. The English keeps every term and does not hedge any of it. Style guide 12: the publication decision, and any framing, belong to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office. Note that the passage is immediately preceded by pages of the Sheikh defending and commending the veneration of the Prophet's relics, traces and household, and by his own account of hearing al-Shifā thirteen times in Rabīʿ al-Awwal — the argument is a boundary-drawing one, not a rejection of love and reverence, and excerpting the rejection alone inverts it.

flags.arabic: فقال له: امصص بظر اللات ويلك أنفر ونترك رسول الله (ص)
flags.context: Abu Bakr's reply to Urwah ibn Masʿud at al-Hudaybiyah.
options: Translate the imprecation literally, as the sources have it
Render it euphemistically
Omit it
flags.note: The imprecation is obscene in Arabic and is in al-Bukhari verbatim; the Sheikh quotes it as it stands. It has been translated literally rather than softened, because softening would remove the point — that even Abu Bakr, the mildest of the Companions, answered in the harshest terms of the pre-Islamic idiom when the Prophet was slighted. A display intended for a general audience may wish to set it behind a note. It is not gratuitous and it is not the Sheikh's own speech.

flags.arabic: حتى إن اليهود بني قريظة حين قال لهم: يا إخوان القردة والخنازير، قالوا يا أبا القاسم ما عهدناك فحاشا
flags.context: In the list of his character traits, as evidence of his known gentleness.
options: Translate the report as it stands and flag
Omit the address
Add an interpretive gloss in the body
flags.note: EDITORIAL. The address to the Banu Qurayzah is in the sīrah material and is reported here in the Sheikh's own argument, whose point is the opposite of an insult in general: the Companions of Qurayzah themselves answered that this was uncharacteristic of him, which is precisely the Sheikh's evidence that gentleness was his known habit. Lifted out of that argument the sentence reads as a slur on a community. Translated exactly; nothing added or removed.

Correct to Hind ibn Abi Halah
flags.note: The famous description of the Prophet's physical form transmitted through al-Hasan ibn Ali comes from his maternal uncle Hind ibn Abi Halah, Khadijah's son. 'Hind ibn Hind' appears to be a slip. Reproduced as spoken.

flags.arabic: خلقك الله بيمينه ونفخ فيك من روحه وأسجد لك ملائكته
flags.context: Inside the hadith of the Greatest Intercession, in what the people say to Adam.
options: Render the report literally without adding a theological gloss, and flag

flags.note: Style guide 8: creedal material about the divine attributes, not a legal ruling. The Sheikh quotes the hadith without glossing 'with His right hand', and the English does the same. flags.arabic: أن رجلا من كبار الموظفين في دولتنا هذه مع احترامنا لكبار الموظفين … أنا أظن أن الحديث يكفي منه دلائل الخيرات الذي عند أمك
flags.context: Illustrating the displacement of hadith study by devotional formularies.
options: Translate the anecdote in full, including the aside of respect
Generalise it so no state is named
flags.note: The Sheikh tells the story about an unnamed senior official of his own country and inserts his own parenthesis of respect. Nobody is identified. Translated in full, including the parenthesis, since removing it would make the anecdote sharper than he made it. Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt is al-Jazuli's widely used collection of formulas of prayer upon the Prophet; the Sheikh's target in the surrounding passage is the substitution of such collections for the study of hadith, not the practice of praying upon the Prophet.

flags.arabic: وقد زعم أبو محمد بن حزم رحمه الله أن الصحابة جميعا يجب الإيمان بأنهم من أهل الجنة
flags.context: After the discussion of knowing the Companions.
options: Render zaʿama as 'claimed', keeping the Sheikh's distance
Render it as 'held' or 'stated'
flags.note: Zaʿama carries a mild distancing in the Sheikh's usage — he reports Ibn Hazm's position and its two proof-texts without endorsing or rejecting it, and moves straight on. 'Claimed' keeps that distance; 'held' would read as agreement. The Sheikh gives no verdict on the question here.

flags.arabic: وكان لمعاوية بن أبي سفيان أظافر النبي (ص)، احتفظ بها فلما أدركه الموت أوصى أن تجعل داخل جفنيه في عينيه
flags.context: In the long passage on the Companions' preservation of the Prophet's relics.
options: Translate the relic reports exactly as narrated and flag the tension with the later passage
Move the relic passage next to the passage on excess
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. This passage and the passage on excess (the first flag) are the two poles of the lecture and must be displayed together. Here the Sheikh commends at length the Companions' and the caliphs' keeping of the Prophet's hair, nails, swords, turban, letters and the traces of his route; there he rejects grave-festivals, mawlid-festivals, istighāthah and hadith-fabrication. His own line between the two is drawn by the sunnah and by what the first generations actually did — not by a general suspicion of veneration. Either passage taken alone misrepresents the lecture.

flags.context: The structure of the intercession section.
options: Keep the Sheikh's numbering exactly as he gives it
Renumber for consistency
flags.note: The Sheikh announces eight intercessions and then names them out of numerical order: he gives the Greatest first, then 'the smallest', then 'the third', 'the fourth kind', 'the fifth', 'the sixth', 'the seventh' and 'the eighth'. The one he calls 'the smallest' is therefore the second in his sequence. His numbering is preserved exactly; a display should not renumber it.

This is a complete lecture transcript. It opens with the basmalah and 'ammā baʿd' and ends on the closing verses of al-Majlisi's poem, with the Sheikh saying that time is an enemy that takes him out of the Prophet's qualities. There is no question-and-answer session in the record.

This record uses '(ص)' throughout as an abbreviation for the prayer upon the Prophet, as IDs 478, 481, 486, 487 and 491 do. The English expands it to '(ṣ)'; body_ar preserves the abbreviation as published. The record also frequently omits the space after it ('(ص)شرفه', '(ص)أنه'), which is preserved.

Unlike the other records in this slice, this one marks Qur'anic quotation with the ornate brackets ﴿ ﴾ rather than curly braces, with one mismatched place that is flagged. The English uses curly braces throughout for consistency with the rest of the corpus.

The lecture's structure, which a display should keep visible, is the one the title announces: the controls, the causes and the manners of loving the Prophet. It runs: (1) love of him as a condition of faith, with its hadith evidence, extended to love of the Helpers and the Companions; (2) the first ground of love — God's choosing of him, with the hadith of successive selection; (3) the second ground — his beneficence, expounded through the eight intercessions, which occupies about a quarter of the lecture; (4) the third ground — his perfection in himself; (5) the controls: that love is an act of the heart and not merely obedience, is not nullified by sin but only diminished, and issues in the three requisites of the shahādah; (6) that love comes only through knowledge, hence the shamāʾil literature, the books of sīrah and ṭabaqāt, and al-Shifā; (7) a long anthology of how the Companions and those after them actually loved him; (8) the boundary — what is excess and what is fabrication; (9) that love requires learning the sunnah; and (10) the shamāʾil proper, of character and of physical form.

EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED. Four passages: the rejection of grave-festivals, the mawlid, tawassul-fabrications and istighāthah; Abu Bakr's obscene imprecation at al-Hudaybiyah; the address to the Banu Qurayzah; and the anecdote about a senior official of the Sheikh's own country. All four are translated exactly and none is softened. Style guide 12.

The chain of transmission the Sheikh recites from his own grandfather back to al-Bukhari has been transliterated name by name rather than summarised, because the point of reciting it is the chain itself: he gives it immediately before the hadith forbidding lying against the Prophet, as a demonstration of what it means to transmit responsibly. One name in it, 'ابن اعل مم السباعي', is a Mauritanian name whose vocalisation is not settled by the text; it has been transliterated conservatively as 'Ibn Aʿl Mamm al-Sibaʿi'.

The record quotes a great deal of Mauritanian (Shinqiti) verse that is not otherwise well known: Shaykh Muhammad Ali, al-Badawi, Shaykh Bab ibn al-Shaykh Sidiyya (two poems), Shaykh Muhammadhu ibn Habib al-Rahman, Abd Allah ibn Sayyid Mahmud, and the closing poem of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad Salim al-Majlisi. It also quotes al-Abbas's praise poem and Abu Talib's lāmiyyah. All have been rendered as verse, line by line, with the hemistich break of the source (**) shown as //. These are working renderings of sense, not metrical English, and a reviewer with access to the dīwāns may wish to revisit several lines — particularly in the al-Majlisi poem, which is dense with place names (al-ʿAqiq, al-Munqa, Uhud, Salʿ, al-Jamma, Yamʾud) and with camel vocabulary.

The Sheikh's own chain of learning is visible in the record and is worth preserving for the corpus: he names his grandfather Muhammad Ali ibn Abd al-Wadud and Shaykh Muhammad Ali, from whom he says he heard al-Shifā thirteen times in Rabīʿ al-Awwal.
